title: Answer to Question: The Leaking of Intelligence Documents and the Position towards Pakistan
text:
Answer to Question: The Leaking of Intelligence Documents and the Position towards Pakistan

Question:

A huge media aura has been raised around the leaking of official intelligence documents through the editor-in-chief of WikiLeaks, especially with regard to Obama's strategy in pursuing the war in Afghanistan and Pakistan. Does the leaking of those documents truly represent a great threat to Obama's war in these two countries? And do David Cameron's recent statements regarding Pakistan and its export of terrorism have a connection with the matter?

Answer:

Before answering this question, the following points must be noted:

1- It is no longer a secret that the strategy of President George Bush's administration in managing the Afghan war failed miserably. Bush's strategy relied on supporting Karzai and conferring legitimacy on his rule and his ability to govern, improving the capability of the Afghan army, including moderate elements of the Pashtun resistance in the government, and exerting pressure on Pakistan to move against the Taliban and other militants residing in the tribal areas. When Obama assumed power in 2009, he asked his administration to carry out a complete review of Bush's strategy.

Obama's initial strategy can be summed up in that it kept the basic principles that Bush had adopted, while increasing the number of American soldiers participating in the war, raising the pace of the attacks directed by drones against the militants on Pakistani territory, and placing additional pressures on the Pakistani army to carry out operations in the tribal areas, particularly in the Waziristan region. There were other modifications in the strategy, such as attempting to reduce civilian casualties and strengthening civilian institutions, in order to make this strategy more acceptable to local and international public opinion.

Nevertheless, Obama's continuous pursuit of reducing the number of American forces deployed in Afghanistan by 2011 has continuously undermined the strategy, stirred up debate between the Obama administration and the American military commanders in the field, and deepened the disagreements between the allies and other regimes such as the Afghan and Pakistani regimes. From Obama's point of view, the timetable for withdrawal is essential for boosting the Democratic Party's electoral chances to compete effectively in the American presidential elections of 2012. However, a number of military and political leaders have strongly objected to the Obama administration over its many demands of the American army within a period that is unrealistic in their view. The most prominent of those voices was the voice of McChrystal, who was forced into early retirement from the American army. Even with General Petraeus taking his place, Petraeus is not able to go ahead completely with implementing the current Afghan strategy, and was compelled to make further modifications to some of the clauses of this strategy. Several statements were issued by Karzai urging the coalition forces to remain and bring about stability in Afghanistan beyond 2011, while Pakistan protested strongly that America would abandon Afghanistan once again and leave Pakistan facing the ferocious war with the Pashtuns on both sides of the border. Consequently, before the leaks, the Obama administration had faced, in addition to the bitter complaints of its followers, growing opposition within the government, the political class and the American army.

2- During the past nine years the United States worked tirelessly to force Pakistan to play a greater role in bringing about stability in Afghanistan. This meant that the leadership of the Pakistani army had to struggle to change the mentality of its army so that it would wage war against its own citizens living in the tribal area. Musharraf's role was essential in this regard, and when he was no longer able to serve his American masters, they removed him and Kayani replaced him, in the hope on their part that he would be more effective than his predecessor; to the extent that the Americans forced the Pakistani government to extend his term as Chief of Army Staff for another three years. Pakistan's Prime Minister Gilani said at the time of Kayani's renewal: "The success of the military operations achieved under the leadership of General Ashfaq Kayani would not have succeeded without his leadership," and he said that "these operations are at a critical stage, and the continued success of these operations requires continuity in the top military leadership." [Financial Times 23/7/2010] Nevertheless, the Americans were disappointed by Kayani's efforts in mobilising the Pakistani army to support the American military operations in Kandahar by moving against the Pakistani Taliban movement in North Waziristan, as well as moving against the other armed groups. Despite the many recent visits of American officials to Pakistan and the provision of civilian and military aid to Pakistan, Kayani failed to achieve tangible successes against the Taliban movement and the militants to limit their use of Pakistani territory. This failure delayed the start of the Kandahar operation and affected Obama's pledge during his election campaign to withdraw American forces from Afghanistan.

3- The obvious failure of the Obama administration in Afghanistan, especially as this failure was accompanied by massacres of civilians, resulted in the Republicans opening fire on Obama's policy in Afghanistan... and Obama came to fear the effect of these voices in weakening the Democratic Party's chances in the coming elections, whether the midterm elections at the end of this year or the presidential elections of 2012 CE.

It was in precisely this circumstance that the uproar of the documentary leaks was raised.

4- By a careful examination of the documents that were leaked, numbering 90,000 or so, we notice that they did not reveal new information about the strategy of the United States in Afghanistan or Pakistan. Rather, the great majority of the documents relating to Afghanistan and Pakistan criticise the policies that Bush pursued. This is not surprising, since the documents are dated before Obama took up his office and announced his strategy towards Afghanistan and Pakistan. Therefore the leaking of these documents exposes the faults of the Bush administration and not the Obama administration, which makes the explanation for the exaggerated reactions of the United States of America to the leaking of the documents that the leak was engineered by the Obama administration in the White House.

This is confirmed by what was published on the website "salon.com" on 27/7/2010 CE, that two New York Times editors, Mark Mazzetti and Eric Achmitt ("Mark Mazzetti and Eric Achmitt"), had gone to the White House a week before that date to brief the administration on what was intended to be published. And they all got gold stars! The website adds their saying: "We did that to give the administration the opportunity to comment and respond, and they did. They also praised us for the way we dealt with the documents, and because we gave them the opportunity to discuss the matter, and for our handling of the information with care as being a responsibility."

[New York Times reporters met with White House before publishing WikiLeaks story, Salon, Jul 27 2010, http://www.informationclearinghouse.info/article26025.htm].

5- On the basis of what has been mentioned above, we can answer the question that the Obama administration is the one that deliberately leaked those old intelligence documents, for two purposes:

The first: domestic, to show the opponents of the American administration that the basis of the failure lies in the era of the previous administration, and here are the documents proving that, and that it was that previous policy which made him carry out a comprehensive review last autumn. This is what Obama declared when he said: "While I am concerned about the disclosure of sensitive information from the battlefield that could threaten individuals or operations, the truth is that these documents do not reveal any issues that had not previously been discussed with the general public regarding the Afghan matter. Indeed, they point to the very challenges that pushed me to carry out a comprehensive review of our policy last autumn." [BBC Online 27/7/2010].

The second: external, to put more pressure on Kayani to mobilise the Pakistani army to move against the Taliban and the Haqqani group located in North Waziristan. It must be pointed out here that before Kayani came as Musharraf's successor, he was the head of Pakistani intelligence between 2004 and 2007. Hence the leaking of those documents is an embarrassment for Kayani.

6- As for David Cameron's comments about Pakistan's hypocrisy, they have another aspect. They are to put pressure on Pakistan and to appear in the guise of a supporter of American policy in Afghanistan, whereas what is intended "from behind a curtain", as is the habit of British policy, is to embarrass Pakistan before the American people, in an attempt on its part to sow discord between the American administration and Pakistan when the American people learn that Pakistani intelligence supports the Taliban in killing Americans!

This is in addition to the fact that any statement that shakes Pakistan as a state by branding it with hypocrisy strengthens the position of India, Britain's ally, and attracts the loyalty of the general Indian people, and not only of the Congress Party government loyal to Britain, because any position against Pakistan on the part of Britain increases the solidity of the British-Indian relationship. This is especially so since Cameron was accompanied on his visit to India by a large trade delegation from the current British government, to address the economic contraction by establishing strong trade relations with other countries, the most prominent of them India, where there is a growing economic market; so strengthening the friendly relations between the two countries is reflected in economic activity.
